quiz: Think about whether Helm ever deletes history entries, or whether every action, including going back, gets its own new number.
Recall the precedence order: chart defaults, then -f files, then command-line flags. The most specific, latest source wins.
Ask of each line: what happens if the new Pods never get Ready, does it cause downtime, and does anything secret end up in shell history or CI logs?
Use the formula desired = ceil(current x currentMetric / targetMetric) and round up.
A CPU percentage needs two inputs: live usage from the Metrics API and a request value to divide by.
maxSurge controls extra Pods above the target and maxUnavailable controls Pods allowed to be missing. Which pair keeps the count from ever dipping?
Compute allowed disruptions as healthy Pods minus minAvailable. What happens to evictions when that is zero?
Block disks live in a single zone. Think about what the PersistentVolume tells the scheduler about where the Pod may run.
The problem is a disk created in one zone before the Pod is placed. Which setting controls when a volume is bound and provisioned?
RBAC rules name resources exactly. Ask whether reading logs is the same resource as reading the Pod object itself.
Kubernetes only stores a NetworkPolicy; some other component in the cluster has to actually enforce it.
Think of the from: list like a list of alternatives, and of fields inside one item like conditions on a single rule. How do they combine?
Kubelets may be older than the API server but never newer. Which part must therefore move first?
Read the error: Kubernetes no longer serves that apiVersion. Which change makes the chart talk to an API the cluster still knows?
exec and attach need a shell already in the image. Which kubectl command can bring its own image into a running Pod?
interview: Define Helm as a package manager, then explain chart (templates, values.yaml, Chart.yaml), release (an install with revision history) and values overrides.
Explain that rollback re-applies an old manifest as a new revision, nothing is deleted, and that migrations and hook side effects are not undone.
Give the order from chart defaults to -f files to --set, explain that maps merge key by key while lists are replaced, and that null removes a default.
Say why secrets must stay out of values files, then cover options like external Secrets with External Secrets Operator or SOPS with helm-secrets.
Define maxSurge as extra Pods allowed and maxUnavailable as Pods allowed missing, then explain maxUnavailable 0 with maxSurge 1 plus honest readiness probes.
Give the formula with ceil, the 10% tolerance, min/max clamping and scale-down stabilization, then list reasons like missing metrics or CPU requests.
Explain that a PDB limits voluntary disruptions, how allowed disruptions are computed, and common setups that leave zero so drain waits forever.
Cover stable identity, ordered names, the headless Service for per-Pod DNS, and how volumeClaimTemplates make one PVC per Pod that outlives it.
Explain the zonal PV and node affinity, how to check describe pod and node zone labels, fix by restoring zone capacity, and prevent with WaitForFirstConsumer.
Cover separate identities, namespace-scoped Roles with exact verbs, short-lived tokens for CI, read-only access for developers, and testing with kubectl auth can-i.
Start with whether the CNI enforces policy, then check Pod and namespace selection, policyTypes direction, and whether the test traffic really crosses Pods.
Stress one minor version at a time, pre-checks for removed APIs, backups and PDBs, then control plane, add-ons and nodes in small batches.
Cover finding deprecated APIs early with tools like pluto or kubent and metrics, fixing charts in CI, and repairing stored Helm release metadata after.
Tell a story in order: detect, stabilise with rollback, diagnose with evidence, communicate, fix, and a blameless postmortem with concrete actions.
